a gathering of three waves into one. "It is what the Latins called the tenth wave; for every third wave was believed to be the greatest, or, as Festus reports, the tenth. Plato Rep. 5 p. 472 a. δύο κύματε ἐκφυγόντι τὸ μέ μέγιστον καὶ χαλεπώτατον τῆς τρικυμίας ἐπάγεις [you bring upon me the greatest and most difficult wave of the triple wave, after I have escaped two waves]."
where Blomfield collected similar sayings of others in his Glossary.

the reading both here and in the strophe v. 974 is suspect on account of the meter. Schol. ζῶντα πήματα χεόμενα καὶ πολλά [living, pouring, and many sufferings]. τριπάλτων δὲ πηματων, σφοδρῶς πηδησάντων [of thrice-brandished sufferings, violently leaping]. τρίπαλτος [thrice-brandished] is nowhere else read, but δίπαλτος [twice-brandished] more often, for examples of which see Thes. vol. 2 p. 1546.

since it is not apparent how it can be said or formed from παχύς [thick], Bamberger conjectured τριπάχυντον [thrice-thickened], from the verb παχύνω [I thicken], which Aeschylus used improperly in the sense of increasing, Sept. 771 ἀνδρῶν ἀλφηστᾶν ὄλβος ἄγαν παχυνθείς [the wealth of bread-eating men, having grown too thick], and Suppl. 618 Ζηνὸς ἱκεσίου κότον μέγαν προφωνῶν μήποτ᾽ εἰσόπιν χρόνου πόλιν παχύναι [foretelling the great wrath of Zeus of suppliants, lest in time to come it thicken the city]. He calls the δαίμονα [divinity] τριπάχυντον [thrice-thickened] with regard to the three generations (which he enumerates at Ch. 1068-1074), the first of Atreus, the second of Agamemnon, the third which followed of Orestes, as Karsten pointed out, although he followed another conjecture of Bamberger, τριπαλαιστήν [thrice-wrestled]. Blomfield conjectured τριπάλαιον [thrice-ancient]: about which Thomas Magister seems to have thought when he noted, διὰ τὸ εἰς τὸν δαίμονα ἀποτείνεσθαι τὸν παλαιόν · ἐκεῖνος γὰρ αἴτιος καὶ τοῦ φόνου τούτου [because it refers to the ancient divinity; for he is the cause also of this murder].
